clue.text: Two-time Booker-winner attending court with daughter

parts.note: attending a place means being at it
to court someone is to woo them

explanation.surface: A double Booker Prize winner shows up at a court hearing with her daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Atwood won the Booker Prize twice, for The Blind Assassin and The Testaments.

clue.text: "Let those who are in favour with — stars / Of public honour and proud titles boast" (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: "Let those who are in favour with — stars / Of public honour and proud titles boast" (Shakespeare)

parts.words: "Let those who are in favour with — stars / Of public honour and proud titles boast" (Shakespeare)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the possessive that completes the opening lines of Shakespeare's Sonnet 25

explanation.surface: Lines from a Shakespeare sonnet with one word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Quotation clues like this have no wordplay: you supply the word missing from the dash, here from Sonnet 25.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive pronoun completing the line refers back to 'those', the favoured people whose lucky stars bring honour.

clue.text: Perhaps do this to enter Marshalsea with deliveries papa put in transport

definitions.text: Perhaps do this to enter Marshalsea

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries, so deliveries suggests overs

indicators.note: put in tells us the letter for papa is placed inside the word for transport

parts.note: to transport someone emotionally is to send them
P is papa in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is sent to a debtors' gaol after a muddle over parcels and a father's journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marshalsea was a notorious London debtors' prison (Dickens's father was held there), so spending beyond your means could land you inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Spending more than you have runs up debts, and debt was what sent people to the Marshalsea.

clue.text: Bar up above dramatic scenery that Hardy called home

indicators.note: in a down entry, above places the first piece over the second
in a down clue, up means the word for bar is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a bar is a rod
the scenery on a theatre stage is the set

explanation.surface: A description of a theatre backdrop recalling the countryside where Thomas Hardy lived.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hardy was born and lived in this county of south-west England, the heart of his fictional Wessex.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy spent most of his life in this south-western English county, the model for his Wessex.

clue.text: A cold starts to enervate sick old warrior

parts.note: a chill is a cold

indicators.note: starts to tells us to take the opening letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: A heavy cold saps the strength of an ailing veteran soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek hero of the Trojan War, slain by an arrow to the heel, is the classic ancient fighter.

clue.text: Post office innovator is not on the payroll, sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests the words not on the payroll have been put into a sorry jumble

explanation.surface: A former postal pioneer finds, to his regret, that he no longer draws a salary.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist worked for the Post Office for decades and is credited with introducing the pillar box to Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian novelist was a senior Post Office official who brought the roadside pillar box into use.

clue.text: Strangely, ruthless people like Edward Felson

indicators.note: Strangely signals the letters of the next word arranged in an odd new order

explanation.surface: Merciless types, as exemplified by a fictional pool shark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast Eddie' Felson is the pool player in Walter Tevis's novel The Hustler, filmed with Paul Newman.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Felson is the con-artist pool player of Tevis's The Hustler, so he exemplifies such swindlers.

clue.text: Collection of really rich verse with songlike qualities

indicators.note: Collection of says the letters are gathered from inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: An anthology of richly musical poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: A poem of this kind expresses personal feeling in a musical, song-like form.

clue.text: Who put down Belinda using sharpness and moral excellence?

parts.note: an edge is a sharpness, as of a blade or a remark
worth means merit or moral excellence

explanation.surface: A question about who set down a woman called Belinda, using a keen wit and virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' looks like rejecting or killing Belinda; it means wrote down. Maria Edgeworth's novel Belinda appeared in 1801.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Edgeworth wrote the 1801 novel Belinda, so she is the one who set it down on paper.

clue.text: Pirate crew, perhaps, with chests opened by key

indicators.note: opened by means the joined words are split apart and the key goes in the gap

parts.note: a crew is an example of men working together
chests are boxes, or crates
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: A pirate gang breaks open treasure chests with a key.
explanation.walkthrough: Menecrates is a pirate in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, an ally of Pompey.
explanation.definitionFit: In Antony and Cleopatra this character is one of the famous pirates who sides with Pompey.

clue.text: Paper first to examine account of school hostage crisis

parts.note: rag is slang for a cheap newspaper

indicators.note: first to tells us to take only the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A newspaper is first on the scene to report a siege at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: Rage is Stephen King's early novel, published as Richard Bachman, about a student who takes his class hostage.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King's novel, written as Richard Bachman, tells of a student holding his classmates captive.

clue.text: Soprano in the thrall of right old charmer

indicators.note: in the thrall of means held captive by, so the letter for soprano sits inside the word for right

parts.note: proper means right or correct
S is the abbreviation for soprano in music

explanation.surface: A singer falls under the spell of an old-fashioned seducer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charmer' suggests a seducer; here it means one who casts charms, the magician of The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: The exiled duke of The Tempest is a magician who works by spells and charms.

clue.text: You and I must track old goat and antelope

indicators.note: to track is to follow, so the word for you and I comes after

parts.note: an old goat is a lecherous man, a lech
you and I together are we

explanation.surface: The two of us have to follow a randy old man and a deer-like creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old goat' and 'antelope' make the clue look like a list of animals; the goat is a lecherous man.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a marsh-dwelling antelope of southern Africa.

clue.text: Regularly lambasted Welsh linesman

indicators.note: Regularly says to take every other letter, here the second, fourth, sixth and eighth

explanation.surface: A Welsh football official is often given a dressing-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' suggests a football official; it means a writer of lines, the Welsh poet Dannie Abse.
explanation.definitionFit: Dannie Abse was a Welsh poet, and a poet writes lines of verse.

clue.text: Completely dark forest? He might set a story in that!

definitions.text: He might set a story in that!

parts.note: completely dark means black
a wood is a forest

explanation.surface: A pitch-black forest is just the place for a spooky tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Algernon Blackwood wrote supernatural fiction such as The Willows and The Wendigo, often set in eerie wilderness.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon Blackwood was a master of the ghost story, so a dark wood suits his tales.

clue.text: Detectives going to prison to see Edward Bunker, perhaps

parts.note: the Yard, short for Scotland Yard, is the London police detective force
bird is British slang for a prison sentence, from rhyming slang 'birdlime' for time

explanation.surface: Police go to a jail to visit a crime writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Bunker was an American career criminal who became a novelist and actor after years in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunker served long prison terms before writing, so he was a seasoned convict, which is slang for a jailbird.

clue.text: Queer writer digs being on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means the word is heard spoken rather than seen written

parts.note: an animal digs burrows

explanation.surface: A gay author tunnels away while broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: William S. Burroughs wrote the novel Queer, so the capital Q names the book.
explanation.definitionFit: William S. Burroughs wrote the short novel Queer, published in 1985.

clue.text: "Vicious, - , foolish, blunt, unkind; / Stigmatical in making, worse in mind" (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: "Vicious, - , foolish, blunt, unkind; / Stigmatical in making, worse in mind" (Shakespeare)

parts.words: "Vicious, - , foolish, blunt, unkind; / Stigmatical in making, worse in mind" (Shakespeare)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing adjective comes from Adriana's list of insults in The Comedy of Errors

explanation.surface: Lines from a Shakespeare comedy with one word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay here: supply the missing word from Adriana's tirade in The Comedy of Errors, Act 4 Scene 2.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective means rough or lacking courtesy, fitting a list of harsh faults.

clue.text: Captain who lost his son in fish restaurant in LA

parts.note: the gar is a long-snouted fish
a diner is a typically American roadside restaurant

explanation.surface: A sea captain mourns his lost boy over seafood at a Los Angeles eatery.
explanation.walkthrough: In Moby-Dick, Captain Gardiner of the Rachel begs Ahab to help search for his son, lost at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: In Melville's Moby-Dick the master of the Rachel is searching the sea for his missing boy.

clue.text: Not all fear a huge sun and moon-eating demon

indicators.note: Not all says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: People don't all dread an enormous monster that devours the heavenly bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu myth this severed head swallows the sun or moon, explaining eclipses.

clue.text: The end of this would be R for Lime's creator

definitions.text: The end of this would be R for Lime's creator

parts.words: The end of this would be R for Lime's creator
parts.note: Harry Lime's creator is Graham Greene, who wrote The End of the ..., and the last letter of the missing word is R

explanation.surface: A remark that something's ending is the letter R, according to the author who invented Harry Lime.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lime is the villain of The Third Man, written by Graham Greene; Greene also wrote The End of the Affair, and the word's final letter is R.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's novel title supplies the word, and its last letter, literally its end, is R.

clue.text: Awful jokes written about parking in a foreign capital

indicators.note: written about means the rearranged letters are set down around the letter for parking
Awful says the letters of the word jokes are mangled into a new order

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for parking on road signs

explanation.surface: Terrible gags are told about finding a parking spot in an overseas city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' makes SKOJE from JOKES, and 'written about' puts P inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Skopje is the capital city of North Macedonia.

clue.text: Those leading prayer sing a lovely mass as well as this!

definitions.text: Those leading prayer sing a lovely mass as well as this!

indicators.note: Those leading points to the opening letters of the five words that follow

explanation.surface: Worship leaders sing a beautiful Mass along with a sacred song.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a sacred song sung in worship alongside the Mass.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacred song of praise is sung in services, alongside prayers and the Mass.

clue.text: Story about female characterised by good ohilosophical work

indicators.note: about means the word for story goes round the letter for female

parts.note: a story can be a lie
of means characterised by, as in a man of honour
pi, short for pious, is crossword shorthand for good

explanation.surface: A tale about a woman marked by goodness turns out to be a weighty book of ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ohilosophical' is the clue's typo for 'philosophical'. Yann Martel's Booker-winning novel is a fable about faith and storytelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Yann Martel's novel is a fable exploring faith, survival and the nature of storytelling.

clue.text: One who constructed a gothic castle for European beneath mountain

definitions.text: One who constructed a gothic castle

indicators.note: in a down entry, beneath puts the letter for European under the mountain

parts.note: a peak is a mountain

explanation.surface: A European builds a dark castle at the foot of a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: Mervyn Peake created the vast gothic castle of Gormenghast in his trilogy of novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Mervyn Peake invented, in fiction, the sprawling castle of Gormenghast.

clue.text: Nana's papa heads to old local alehouse after bit of sleep

indicators.note: after places the opening letters of old, local and alehouse following the sleep letter

parts.note: Z, as in catching some zeds, stands for a bit of sleep

indicators.note: heads to tells us to take the opening letters of the three words that follow

explanation.surface: Grandma's dad heads for the old local pub after a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nana' looks like a grandmother; it is Emile Zola's novel Nana, so her 'papa' is her author.
explanation.definitionFit: Emile Zola wrote the novel Nana, so he fathered the character as her author.

clue.text: One who worked in a cemetery a ghost army startled

definitions.text: One who worked in a cemetery

indicators.note: startled suggests the letters of a ghost army have jumped into a new order

explanation.surface: A gravedigger is frightened by a spectral host of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet wrote Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, so he 'worked' in a graveyard.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century poet composed his famous Elegy in a country churchyard.

clue.text: A mum given the sack by English carpenter of some repute

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother
hitting the sack means going to bed

explanation.surface: A mother is dismissed by an English joiner of good name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given the sack' suggests being fired; the sack is bed. George Eliot's hero Adam Bede is a carpenter.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's title hero is a carpenter respected for his skill and integrity.

clue.text: Artist that woman gets piece from Renoir and a Bacon piece

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword abbreviation for an artist
that woman means she

indicators.note: piece from tells us to take one letter, the first, from the painter's name

explanation.surface: A female painter takes a fragment of a Renoir and a painting by Francis Bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacon piece' looks like a work by the painter Francis Bacon, prompted by Renoir; it is a slice of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: A slice cut from a side of bacon is the breakfast portion meant.
